open-question.question: This mission refuses a new Short Title holding a `/` at `add`, because the alternatives agent writes its return to a file named by the title. Most fixed calls also substitute the title inside a double-quoted shell argument, where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special, and only the answer sweep's batched call states an escaping rule for it. Which further characters, if any, does `add` refuse in a new Short Title: none, those four, or everything outside an allow-list of letters, digits, spaces, and a fixed set of punctuation?
open-question.alternative: `add` refuses no character beyond the `/` the mission already refuses: `"`, `$`, backtick, `\`, and control characters are all accepted in a new Short Title, and every fixed call keeps substituting the title as an unescaped literal inside double quotes, the double-quoted positions recorded as an accepted gap. No title anyone writes is refused for a character that has never broken anything here: every id in this repository's history uses only letters, digits, spaces, `-`, and `.` (one escaping test fixture aside), and the tool, its help text, and the review pass's rule gain nothing beyond the slash check. A title holding `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\` still breaks or silently changes the argument at every double-quoted call but the sweep's, a backtick running its text as a command, and a control character passes `add` and leaves `open_questions.xml` malformed so that every later tool call on the mission is refused (checked on 2026-11-25 with `\x01`); whether a `"` also breaks the recommendation pass's hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses no character beyond `/`; instead the sweep's rule, that every title written inside double quotes has any `"`, `$`, backtick, or `\` escaped by a backslash, is stated at every other fixed call and procedure step that substitutes a Short Title (the review pass's `add` and `remove`, the recommendation pass's `embed`, `lift`, and `printf`, the answer core's `locate`, `remove`, and `lift`, the `strip` calls); control characters stay accepted. No title is ever refused, and the shell positions are closed where they break, in the same form the sweep already uses and its batched-call test already pins, so the set of characters a title may hold stays open. Correctness rests on every runner escaping correctly at a dozen sites, most of them in calls no fixed-call test extracts, which is the per-runner escaping the tools exist to remove; a control character still corrupts the document at `add`, and whether a `"` still breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, every control character (C0 and DEL) in the folded title, the one class that makes the tool itself write a malformed document; `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` stay accepted and the double-quoted positions stay as they are, recorded as an accepted gap. It closes the one failure that damages state rather than one call, a title that leaves `open_questions.xml` unreadable to every later tool call, at the cost of refusing nothing a person would write, so no recorded or plausible title is affected. The four double-quote characters keep breaking or silently changing every fixed call but the sweep's, a backtick running as a command, and whether a `"` breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, every control character (C0 and DEL); the four double-quote characters stay accepted and the sweep's backslash-escaping rule is stated at every other fixed call and procedure step that substitutes a Short Title. The document can no longer be corrupted by a title, and the shell positions are closed without refusing any printable character, so a title may still hold a quote, a dollar sign, or a backslash. The shell positions still rest on every runner escaping correctly at a dozen sites, most of them untested, and the rule must be written into each of them; whether a `"` still breaks the hand-rendered attributes depends on how that sibling question settles.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, the four characters special inside double quotes, `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\`, in the folded title, a deny-list of five; control characters stay accepted and the fixed calls stay as shown, with no escaping rule needed for a new title. It closes both named uses of the title, the file name and the double-quoted argument, with one check of the same shape as the slash refusal, refusing characters no recorded title has ever held, so every call site stays exactly as shown. A control character still passes `add` and leaves the document unreadable to every later call, and the deny-list names only the failures found so far, so a position found later needs another addition; blocks authored before it keep their titles, a case a sibling question owns.

`add` refuses, beside `/`, the four double-quote characters `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` and every control character (C0 and DEL) in the folded title; the fixed calls stay as shown, with no escaping rule needed for a new title. Every failure known for a Short Title is closed at its one creation point, the file name, the double-quoted argument, and the malformed document, while every printable character outside the four stays allowed, so no title a person would plausibly write is refused. It is still a deny-list of the failures found so far, so a later-found position needs another addition, and the refusal message and the review pass's rule must name a longer set; blocks authored before it keep their titles, a case a sibling question owns.

`add` refuses every character of the folded title outside an allow-list: letters and digits as Unicode classes them, the space, and a fixed set of punctuation (for instance `-`, `_`, `.`, `,`, `'`, `(`, `)`, `:`, `?`), which leaves out `/`, the four double-quote characters, control characters, and any other symbol; the fixed calls stay as shown. It closes the whole class rather than the failures found so far, so a position discovered later cannot break on a character a title may hold, and every recorded title, which uses only letters, digits, spaces, `-`, and `.`, still passes. It refuses characters no one has shown to break anything (an em dash, `&`, `+`, `#`), the punctuation set is one more fixed list the tool and the review pass's rule must state, and whether `.` and a leading `-` belong in it depends on how the separator and leading-dash sibling questions settle.

open-question.question: Once `add` refuses certain characters in a new Short Title, where is the rule stated: only in the open-question tool's help text and `Error:` line, with the review pass's Short Title rule naming the refusal as it names the duplicate-id refusal, or also as a statement in that rule of what a Short Title may hold, so the author writes a valid title the first time?
open-question.alternative: The refusal is stated only by the open-question tool: its module docstring and `add` help text name the refused characters, and its `Error:` line names the one a refused title holds. The Short Title bullet in `review-mission-requirements` is left as it stands, naming only the duplicate-id refusal, and no other runtime file mentions the character rule. The character set has one home, the tool that enforces it, so no prose copy can drift from it when the set changes. It also fits the rule that runtime prose states a tool's contract in at most one sentence per site. The cost is low: none of the 478 recorded block ids holds `/`, `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\`, a refused `add` leaves the document byte-identical, and the author only retries with the `Error:` line in hand. The author learns the rule only from a refusal. The draft's trigger, `tools/README.md headroom`, shows that a path-like title comes naturally when a question concerns one file, so each such title costs the review pass an extra turn. The bullet also stays silent about a refusal that sits right beside the duplicate-id one it already names.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule as in the tool-only form. The review pass's Short Title bullet gains one clause naming the refusal the way it names the duplicate-id refusal: the tool refuses a title holding a character it cannot carry, its `Error:` line names it, and the author picks another title and calls again. The clause lists no characters. The bullet now tells the author that a character refusal exists and how to recover, in the same shape as the duplicate-id clause. The character set stays in the tool alone, so whatever set the refusal ends up holding needs no prose change. Without the characters, the author still cannot avoid them up front, so the first path-like or quoted title is still refused and retried. The clause mostly repeats what the `Error:` line already says when it fires.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule. The review pass's Short Title bullet gains one clause naming the refusal and listing the characters `add` refuses, framed as a refusal: the tool refuses a title holding any of them, its `Error:` line names the one found, and the author picks another title. The author can avoid every refused character before the first call, so a valid title is written the first time. The clause also keeps the shape the bullet already uses for the duplicate-id refusal, a statement of what the tool refuses rather than a new authoring rule. The character set now has two homes, the tool and the review pass's prose, and they must change together or the prose will name a set the tool no longer enforces. How long the clause is depends on how many characters the sibling question on refused characters settles: a short list for `/` or the four shell-active characters, an unwieldy one if the set is defined by an allow-list.

The tool's help text and `Error:` line state the rule. The review pass's Short Title bullet also gains a positive statement of what a Short Title may hold, as an authoring rule: plain words of the characters the tool accepts, with a file or path the question concerns named by its role in the title and written out in the question text. The tool's refusal is named after that statement as the backstop, with the author picking another title on its `Error:` line. It meets the question's aim of a valid title on the first attempt most directly. It tells the author not only which characters to avoid but how to phrase a title about one file, which is the case that triggered the draft. A rule stated in terms of what is allowed also reads naturally if the accepted set is an allow-list. It adds an authoring rule beside the bullet's existing ones and a second statement of the character set, which must track the tool's set exactly. Rules on phrasing are judgment that no test pins. How well it fits depends on the sibling questions on refused characters and on the answer-text separator: for example, whether a `.`, and with it every file name, is ruled out of a title.

open-question.question: The refusal of characters in a Short Title runs only at `add`, so a block authored before it keeps its title, and a title holding a `/` fails the alternatives agent's file write on every run, leaving the block without alternatives. What happens to an existing block whose Short Title a new `add` would refuse: is it left as it stands, to be re-authored by hand, or does the review pass re-author it under a valid title as cleanup?

A task's `##` heading is substituted into double-quoted shell arguments (`--subject "Task-completion: <TASK_NAME>"` in both completion calls, the title arguments of `submit-task` and of the task-list tool's `remove`), where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special; only `submit-task` states an escaping rule, and this repository's recorded headings already hold a double quote. Does the task-list tool refuse those characters in a new task title, as `add` refuses characters in a Short Title, or are task titles handled another way or left as they are?

The commit procedure shows a commit body as the double-quoted literal `--body "<BODY>"`, where a backtick or `$` expands and a `"` ends the argument, and the skills following it pass Markdown text there (the finish summary, a hand answer's rationale, a lifted line); many recorded bodies hold such characters, so each runner has been changing the quoting on its own. How does a body reach the commit tool from the commit procedure: captured from a quoted heredoc and passed as a quoted variable, as the completion calls do, read by the tool from standard input or a file, or written as a literal under a stated escaping rule?
open-question.alternative: The commit procedure's shown command changes to the form the completion calls already use: the body is captured once from a quoted heredoc in the group-fed form `{ body="$(cat)"; } <<'EOF'`, under the clause telling the runner to pick a delimiter line the text does not contain, and passed on as `--body "$body"` in the same shell call, a BODY-less caller leaving both the capture and `--body` out as it leaves out `--body` now. The commit tool and its contract stay unchanged, every caller following the procedure by reference (`finish-mission`, `answer-open-question`, the two lift-based answer skills, `capture-mission-principle-updates`) gets the form through the procedure with no edit of its own, the fixed calls that already pass a captured value keep their calls, and the new command is pinned by a test extracting it from the rendered tree and running it on a body holding a backtick, a `$`, a `"`, and an apostrophe. It closes the expansion with no tool change and no revised invariant: the form is the one the shell-commands invariant already scopes as a single quoted value outside the variable ban and the one both completion calls run, so the plugin ends with one body-passing shape and the runner types the Markdown verbatim with nothing to escape. The text still passes through the shell, so it rests on the delimiter clause (a body line equal to the delimiter ends the heredoc and runs the rest as commands) and on the runner keeping the group-fed form, since the nested `$(cat <<'EOF'` form fails on bash 3.2 when the body holds an apostrophe; command substitution also drops the body's trailing newlines, harmless for git but a silent normalization.

The commit tool gains a standard-input body form (a flag such as `--body-stdin`, or `--body -`), and the commit procedure's command feeds BODY to it directly as a quoted heredoc, under the delimiter clause, with no shell variable in between; `--body` stays for the fixed calls that already pass a captured value (`$bar`, `$pick`, `$body`, the orchestrator's `$(cat "<scratch dir>/body.txt")`), which are left as they are. The tool's help text, its tests, and the committing invariant's statement that the tool gained no body option of its own are revised, and the procedure's command is pinned by an extracting test. It puts the commit tool on the plugin-wide convention every document writer already follows (free text on stdin as a quoted heredoc), so the body never becomes a shell value at all and the procedure's command keeps one process with nothing captured or re-passed. It changes a tool's contract and revises a recorded invariant for a failure a no-tool-change form also closes, leaves the tool with two body inputs whose precedence must be defined and tested, and still rests on the heredoc delimiter clause.

The commit tool takes its body from standard input only, `--body` retired: the commit procedure feeds BODY as a quoted heredoc under the delimiter clause, and every fixed call that passes a body today is rewritten to feed it the same way (both completion calls their heredoc straight to the tool, the orchestrator `< "<scratch dir>/body.txt"`, the sweep and the recommendation pass their held value through `printf '%s'`), with the tool's tests, the four fixed-call tests, and the committing invariant revised to match. One body input across the whole plugin, with no captured bar or held body re-passed through a quoted argument anywhere, so there is no second form for a runner to reach for and no precedence rule to define. It rewrites five working, tested fixed calls and their tests to fix the one site that is not fixed, and the completion calls' capture exists to test the bar for a non-blank line before `remove`, so they would still need the value in hand and the rewrite gains them nothing.

The commit tool gains a `--body-file FILE` option, and the commit procedure has the runner write BODY with its file-writing tool to a file outside the repository (a path made with `mktemp`, held as a path and written out in full, never kept in a shell variable) and then name it on the command line, the shell never touching the text; the orchestrator's `--body "$(cat …)"` may move onto the same option, the other fixed calls keeping `--body`. The tool's help text and tests, the committing invariant's no-body-file clause, and the procedure's command are revised and pinned by tests. It is the only form in which no shell parses the body at all, so no backtick, `$`, quote, apostrophe, or delimiter-looking line can affect it, and it extends the line-exact file read the tool already does for `--path-file`. It costs every committing caller an extra write turn and a temporary location (and since the plugin deletes no scratch file, a leftover body file per commit), and it reverses the committing invariant's explicit decision that the tool gained no body-file option.

The command stays the double-quoted literal `--body "<BODY>"`, and the commit procedure gains the escaping rule the answer sweep and `submit-task` already state for titles: every `"`, `$`, backtick, and `\` in BODY is escaped by a backslash; no tool changes, and a test fills the procedure's command through a helper applying the rule. It is the smallest edit, one sentence in one procedure, and it makes the body follow the same escaping rule the plugin already states for titles and headings, so a runner meets one quoting rule everywhere a literal is substituted. Correctness rests on every runner escaping every character of a Markdown body, and finish summaries and lifted lines are dense with backticks; one missed backtick runs its text as a command and the commit still lands with a mangled body and exit 0, the failure the question exists to close.

The command writes BODY as a single-quoted literal, `--body '<BODY>'`, and the commit procedure states its one escaping rule: every `'` in BODY is written as `'\''`; nothing else is special, no tool changes, and a test fills the command through a helper applying the rule. Only one character needs escaping instead of four, so backticks and `$`, the characters Markdown bodies hold most, pass through untouched with no tool change. Apostrophes are common in English prose and summaries, the `'\''` form is easy to get wrong and hard to read, a missed one still breaks the argument or runs text as shell, and it is a second quoting rule beside the double-quote rule the plugin states for titles.

Nothing changes: the commit procedure keeps the double-quoted literal with no rule, each runner keeps choosing its own quoting as it has been, and CLAUDE.md records the case as accepted with its reason. No edit to the procedure, the tool, or any test, and the field runs show runners already adapting the quoting themselves, so the commits that land mostly carry their bodies intact. The shown command stays wrong for the text it is given, so every runner that copies it literally expands a backtick or `$` or cuts the argument at a `"`, silently and with exit 0, and the run-to-run variation in quoting is exactly the unreproducible behaviour the mission sets out to close.

open-question.question: The answer sweep passes a decision's `###` heading to the fold tool as the double-quoted literal `--section "<Heading>"`, under its rule that `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are escaped by a backslash; an unescaped backticked heading runs its text as a command, exits 0, and creates a mangled subsection, so correctness rests on each runner's escaping. Does the heading keep reaching the tool as an escaped literal, or does it reach it another way: a value captured from a quoted heredoc, standard input, or a file?
open-question.alternative: The heading keeps reaching `fold` and `replace` as the double-quoted literal `--section "<Heading>"` in the sweep's question and conflict sections, under the escaping rule the sweep already states (`"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` escaped by a backslash); no fence, tool, or test changes, and CLAUDE.md records the exposure as accepted, with its reason, as the entry's outcome. Nothing changes and nothing new can break: the rule is already stated at the one site, the existing batched-call test already fills a heading holding characters the quotes must escape, and the field record shows no call ever ran with a raw backtick (12 of the 15 risky headings in 1,076 calls were escaped by the runner as told). Correctness keeps resting on each runner's escaping inside a call it is told to run exactly as shown; one missed backtick runs its text as a command, exits 0, and creates a mangled subsection that `fold` never refuses, and a backticked text naming a real command would run it.

The heading stays a literal on the command line but is written inside single quotes, `--section '<Heading>'`, in both sweep sections, the escaping rule narrowed for that position to one character: a `'` in the heading written as `'\''`; the tool and its contract are unchanged, and the batched-call test's helper fills the heading under the new rule. Inside single quotes `$`, backticks, `"`, and `\` are inert, so the failure the question names (a backticked heading run as a command) can no longer happen through any character but one, with no tool change and the call still one fixed fence. It is still a runner-applied escaping rule, now for the apostrophe, which recorded headings hold often (the tested failing heading itself, `The readers' `tasks` calls`, holds one); a missed `'` closes the quote early and leaves the rest of the heading, backticks included, unquoted, and the position then differs from the double-quoted form every other title, option, and subject in the same call uses.

Each sweep section captures its heading once from a quoted heredoc in the group-fed form the completion calls use for the bar (`{ heading="$(cat)"; } <<'EOF'`, the heading on the one line inside) and passes it on as `--section "$heading"` to `fold` or `replace`; the runner escapes nothing in the heading, the delimiter clause covers the new heredoc, the fold tool and its contract are unchanged, and the batched-call test fills a raw backticked heading through the new form. Nothing the heading holds is ever shell syntax, with no tool change and no escaping left to any runner; the form is one the plugin already ships and tests (both completion calls, at bash 3.2 included), matches what two field runs improvised, and keeps `--section` a required argument as the fold-tool invariant decides. Every section grows by a second heredoc and one more per-section shell variable, which the shell-commands invariant's scoping has to name as it names `pick` and `out`; the Short Title and option in the same section stay escaped literals unless their own questions change them, so the call ends up with two ways of carrying text side by side.

The fold tool takes the heading from standard input together with the body, for example as the first line of the heredoc with the decision below it, in place of the `--section` argument (or beside it under a flag selecting the stdin form), for both `fold` and `replace`; the sweep's sections write the heading inside the heredoc they already have, the tool's help text, contract, and tests change, and CLAUDE.md's fold-tool invariant is revised. The heading travels in the one quoted heredoc each section already carries, so it is never shell syntax, the section gains no line and no variable, and no character of it needs escaping by anyone. It reverses a recorded design decision (`--section` required as an argument, `fold` kept exactly as it was with its contract and six test files untouched), adds a parsing rule to a tool built to treat its stdin as an opaque body, and makes a heading line a decision forgot to write read as its first body line silently becoming the heading.

The fold tool gains an option reading the heading from a file (`--section-file PATH`) for `fold` and `replace`; each sweep section first writes the heading to a file through a quoted heredoc and then passes that file's path, so the sweep needs a scratch location of its own; the tool's contract and tests change and the fold-tool invariant is revised. The heading never appears on a command line at all, so no character of it is shell syntax, and the file form mirrors the line-exact `--path-file` the commit tool already reads, keeping stdin the body's alone. It costs the most of any option: a new tool option, a scratch directory the sweep does not create today, an extra write per section, and the same quoted heredoc the captured-variable form needs anyway, so it adds a file and a tool change for no protection that form lacks.

open-question.question: `answer-open-question` and `answer-open-question-with-alternative` split their text on the first `.`, the Short Title before it, so a Short Title holding a dot (three recorded titles open with `CLAUDE.md`) cannot be named to either, and the answer lines of the extension's recipes and of the usage documents are built on that form. What separates a Short Title from the text after it: is a `.` refused in a new Short Title, is the title matched as the longest existing Short Title the text opens with, or is the separator changed to one a Short Title cannot hold?

The discuss line of the extension's shipped recipes and of the hand-use document appends `. <note>` to the Short Title, but `discuss-open-question` reads the whole text after the flag as the Short Title, so a non-empty note reaches `locate` as part of the title and the run is refused. open-question.alternative: `discuss-open-question` gains a parse rule at its step 0: after the `--mission` strip, the text is split on the same separator the hand-answer skills use (the first `.` today), the part before it the Short Title passed to `locate` and the part after it, trimmed, an optional note the discussion takes as the user's opening remark on the question; text holding no separator is the Short Title alone with no note. The discuss lines in `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md`, `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`, and `gurita-vscode/USAGE.md` and the extension's note prompt and empty-note drop stay as they are. One separator rule for every skill that takes a Short Title followed by text, and the fix sits entirely in the plugin, so the `. <note>` line already bundled into the installed 0.3.0 extension starts working with the next plugin release, with no line or extension change. Discuss inherits the dot separator's failure: a Short Title holding a `.` (three recorded titles open with `CLAUDE.md`), which the skill can name today by reading the whole text as the title, would be cut at its first dot and refused, so the option's soundness rests on how the Answer text separator question settles the separator for the answer skills.

`discuss-open-question` gains a parse rule that separates the note by matching against the document rather than by a separator: the whole text after the `--mission` strip is tried as the Short Title first, and when no block carries it, the title is the longest existing Short Title (case-folded) the text opens with when it is followed directly by `. `, the rest, trimmed, the note the discussion takes as the user's opening remark; text matching neither way is refused as `locate` refuses it today. The discuss lines, the hand-use document, `USAGE.md`, and the extension's note prompt stay as they are. Every Short Title stays nameable to discuss, a dotted one included, with or without a note, and the `. <note>` line already shipped in extension 0.3.0 works with the next plugin release, with no line or extension change. The skill gains a matching rule its siblings lack, read by prose against a whole list of titles rather than by one split, so a runner can misapply it, and discuss then parses its text differently from the answer skills unless the Answer text separator question settles on the same matching form.

The note moves to a flag of its own: `discuss-open-question` gains a rule reading an optional `--note` token after the Short Title, everything before it the title and everything after it the note taken as the user's opening remark, and the discuss lines in `shipped_recipes.md`, `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`, and `USAGE.md` change from `<Short Title>. <note>` to `<Short Title> --note <note>`, the extension's empty-note drop changed to drop ` --note ` with an empty note instead of `. `. The note's boundary is a marker no Short Title holds, so discuss parses every title exactly as it does today, dotted ones included, whatever separator the answer skills end up with. A second flag beside `--mission` with its own recognition rule, a change to the extension's optional-placeholder drop and its tests, and the fixed lines reach installed copies only with a later extension release, which this mission does not make, while installed 0.3.0 keeps sending `. <note>` and keeps being refused.

The discuss lines drop the note: `shipped_recipes.md` and `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` write the discuss line as `--mission <path> <Short Title>` and lose their optional-note sentence, the extension's **Discuss** stops asking for a note and `OPTIONAL_PLACEHOLDERS` loses `note` (with `USAGE.md` and the placeholder tests updated), and the user types any note as the first message of the interactive session the line opens; `discuss-open-question` is unchanged and keeps reading the whole text as the Short Title. The skill keeps its one simple parse, the whole text as the title, so no new rule is added and every title, dotted ones included, stays nameable, while the discussion is interactive anyway, so a note typed after it starts loses nothing the line carried. It removes a feature the extension advertises and changes extension code and tests, and the change reaches installed copies only with a later extension release, which this mission does not make, so installed 0.3.0 keeps sending a non-empty note and keeps being refused until then.

Neither the skill nor the lines change: a non-empty note keeps reaching `locate` inside the Short Title and the run is refused, an empty note keeps working, and CLAUDE.md records the case as accepted with its reason, that the discuss line opens an interactive session where the user sees the refusal and can name the question again. No change to the skill, the shipped lines, the extension, or any test, and no new parsing rule a runner could misapply. The extension's **Discuss** button fails on every non-empty note, so the optional-note prompt it shows and `USAGE.md` documents is a feature that never works, and the mission's goal of closing each mechanical failure is met here only by recording it.

open-question.question: The mission-definition tool accepts a scope holding a space, parentheses, or brackets, while every fixed call writes `<MISSION_DIR>` unquoted and the `--mission` value is read as the one whitespace-separated token after the flag, so such a mission cannot be named or breaks the shell call. Project file paths are written unquoted on the commit tool's command line (`<PATHS>` in the commit procedure, the recorded paths in the inline completion call), so a path holding a space or a shell-active character breaks the call, while the completion agent's path file, read line-exact, is unaffected. An alternative's id is a free-form label the alternatives agent writes, checked at `embed --alternatives` only as non-empty and unique within its block, and it is later substituted into the double-quoted `--option "<Option>"` argument, where `"`, `$`, a backtick, and `\` are special. Does `embed --alternatives` refuse those characters in an alternative id, as `add` refuses characters in a Short Title, or are ids handled another way or left unchecked?
open-question.alternative: `embed --alternatives` refuses an alternative whose id holds `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\`, a fixed set of the id's own that is checked independently of whatever `add` refuses in a Short Title. The check runs at embed only, so ids already in a document stand and loading a document checks no id character. The alternatives agent's rendering rule names the four characters as ones an id may not hold. No call site gains an escaping rule. It closes exactly the shell-active class at the one place ids enter the document. The agent is told the rule up front, so it writes a valid id the first time and a refusal stays rare. No recorded id is affected: none of the 3,853 distinct ids in this repository's history holds any of the four. The rule is stated in two homes, the tool's `Error:` line and the agent's file, and they can drift apart. The ` — ` cut is left to the sibling that owns it. The id's refused set can diverge from the Short Title's, depending on how the sibling on Short Title characters settles.

`embed --alternatives` refuses an id holding `"`, `$`, a backtick, or `\`, checked at embed only and independently of the Short Title rule. The rule is stated only in the open-question tool's help text and its `Error:` line. The alternatives agent's file is unchanged, and no call site gains an escaping rule. The rule has one home, the tool. The agent's file stays as it is, and the existing one-repair loop already hands the agent the `Error:` line to correct against. The commit tool repeats every git write that exits 128, up to 16 attempts over about four seconds, reading only the exit status and never git's message, so a failure no lock caused, such as a pathspec matching no file, is repeated to the last attempt before its error prints. Does the tool keep repeating every exit 128, or does it stop at once on one no lock caused, which needs it to read git's message text or to tell the two cases apart some other way?

The task-list tool, the only writer of `TASKS_TODO.md`, can initialize, insert, and remove but cannot rewrite a section already in the list, and in field runs the list was changed by hand eleven times, most of them a `complete-all-tasks` session rewording a later task's brief after a finding. How is a queued task's brief revised: through a new subcommand rewriting one section's body, as a stated `remove` and `insert` at the same position, or by hand edits accepted for the list?

In field runs 15 of 1,945 `complete-task` agents ended on neither `DONE` nor `FAILED:`, most of them a turn ended while waiting on a background process, and `complete-all-tasks` stops its run on a fixed line when an agent returns no status. Is this closed, by a rule in the agent's file or a step in the orchestrator, or only recorded as accepted?

The `complete-task` agent's file rules out any payload above its bare `DONE`, yet since 2026-11-18 58 of 415 `DONE` returns carried a summary above the token; the orchestrator reads the last line only, so the cost is the text it has to hold. Is this closed by a change to the agent's file, or only recorded as accepted?

Eight alternatives returns were refused as malformed XML in field runs, seven for a mismatched tag and one for a raw element such as `<Link>` written in an alternative's text, each costing its one repair; the agent's rendering rule names `&` and `<` as the characters to write as entities. Is this closed, by a change to the agent's rendering rule or to what the tool accepts, or only recorded as accepted?

`ideas/mechanical_issues.md` stands only as a staged, uncommitted addition beside the staged deletion of `ideas/short_title_characters.md`, the one form of the draft `HEAD` holds, and the mission ends with the draft deleted from `ideas/`; its transcript and history counts are reproduced by no file in the tree. Is the draft committed before it is deleted, so that history keeps its evidence, or does it leave without ever being committed, the earlier draft's deletion committed alone?
